case_info.scenario: A 24-year-old man presented with progressive gait instability. Although this started in childhood as a tendency to drag his left leg and trip, he could keep his balance on a skateboard until the age of 14 years. He had no significant medical history. There was neither family history of neurological illnesses nor consanguinity. Upon neurologic examination, he had normal cognition, slight dysarthria, impaired smooth pursuit, subtle tremor of both hands, left-sided spasticity, normal muscle strength, mildly impaired joint position sense in his toes bilaterally, and hyperreflexia with increased patellar and ankle jerk reflexes. Pes cavus and Babinski sign were present bilaterally as well as truncal and appendicular ataxia. Several teeth were absent (hypodontia) or too small (microdontia). Electrocardiogram results were normal. Complete blood cell count, thyroid, liver, and kidney function were within normal limits. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain and upper spinal cord (Figure 1) showed marked spinal cord atrophy with an anterior-posterior width of 4 mm, isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles, and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum.

case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A 24-year-old man presented with progressive gait instability. Although this started in childhood as a tendency to drag his left leg and trip, he could keep his balance on a skateboard until the age of 14 years. He had no significant medical history. There was neither family history of neurological illnesses nor consanguinity. Upon neurologic examination, he had normal cognition, slight dysarthria, impaired smooth pursuit, subtle tremor of both hands, left-sided spasticity, normal muscle strength, mildly impaired joint position sense in his toes bilaterally, and hyperreflexia with increased patellar and ankle jerk reflexes. Pes cavus and Babinski sign were present bilaterally as well as truncal and appendicular ataxia. Several teeth were absent (hypodontia) or too small (microdontia). Electrocardiogram results were normal. Complete blood cell count, thyroid, liver, and kidney function were within normal limits. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain and upper spinal cord (Figure 1) showed marked spinal cord atrophy with an anterior-posterior width of 4 mm, isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles, and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum.

options.C: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay

case_info.caption: Sagittal fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) (A) and T1-weighted imaging (B) of the brain and upper spinal cord showing marked spinal cord atrophy (A and B, pink arrowhead), isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncle (A, blue arrowhead), and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum (B, blue arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.
